--- title: "Tutorial for the purrr Package" date: "1/6/2025" date-modified: last-modified date-format: long --- # Tutorial for the `purrr` Package ## Introduction ### Overview The `purrr` package, part of the `tidyverse`, provides a set of tools for functional programming in R. It simplifies iteration, mapping, and manipulation of lists, vectors, and other data structures. The functions in `purrr` are designed to replace and enhance base R functions like `lapply()` and `sapply()` with more readable and consistent alternatives. Key components: - **Core Functions**: `map()`, `map2()`, `pmap()`, `reduce()`, `pluck()`, and others. - **Helpers**: `safely()`, `possibly()`, `transpose()`, etc. ### Use Cases - Applying a function to each element of a list or vector. - Handling nested data structures like lists of data frames. - Aggregating results using custom operations. - Safely working with functions that might return errors. ### Benefits - Consistent syntax and predictable outputs. - Seamless integration with other tidyverse packages. - Tools for error handling and debugging. --- ## Getting Started ### Loading the Package Use the `pacman` package to ensure `purrr` is loaded: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(purrr) ``` ::: ### Basic Usage A simple example of applying a function to a list using `map()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define a list numbers <- list(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) # Apply a square function to each element squared <- numbers |> map(~ .x^2) # Print results squared ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] 1 [[2]] [1] 4 [[3]] [1] 9 [[4]] [1] 16 [[5]] [1] 25 ``` ::: ::: Here, `~ .x^2` defines an anonymous function that squares each number. ## Key Functions and Features ### `map()` #### Description The `map()` family applies a function to each element of a list or vector and returns a list, vector, or another type based on the specific `map_*` function used. #### Syntax ```r map(.x, .f, ...) ``` - `.x`: Input list or vector. - `.f`: Function to apply. - `…`: Additional arguments passed to `.f`. #### Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Apply `sqrt()` to each element roots <- list(4, 9, 16) |> map(sqrt) # Print results roots ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] 2 [[2]] [1] 3 [[3]] [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: ### `map2()` #### Description Applies a function to two inputs simultaneously, element by element. #### Syntax ```r map2(.x, .y, .f, ...) ``` #### Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Combine two vectors by addition vector1 <- c(1, 2, 3) vector2 <- c(4, 5, 6) result <- map2(vector1, vector2, ~ .x + .y) result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] 5 [[2]] [1] 7 [[3]] [1] 9 ``` ::: ::: ### `pmap()` #### Description Applies a function to multiple inputs, where inputs are supplied as a list of named arguments. #### Syntax ```r pmap(.l, .f, ...) ``` - `.l`: A list of arguments. - `.f`: Function to apply. #### Example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define inputs inputs <- list(a = c(1, 2, 3), b = c(4, 5, 6), c = c(7, 8, 9)) # Apply a custom function result <- pmap(inputs, \(a, b, c) a + b + c) result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [1] 12 [[2]] [1] 15 [[3]] [1] 18 ``` ::: ::: ## In-Depth Examples ### Title: Aggregating Results Using `reduce()` #### Objective Sum a list of numbers iteratively using `reduce()`. #### Steps 1. **Define the data**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} numbers <- list(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) ``` ::: 2. **Apply `reduce()`**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} total <- reduce(numbers, \(x, y) x + y) total ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15 ``` ::: ::: 3. **Interpret the result**: The sum of the numbers is computed iteratively. ### Title: Handling Errors with `safely()` #### Objective Use `safely()` to apply a function that might fail. #### Steps 1. **Define the data**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} inputs <- list(10, "a", 20) ``` ::: 2. **Use `safely()`**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} safe_sqrt <- safely(sqrt) results <- map(inputs, safe_sqrt) ``` ::: 3. **Inspect results**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} results ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [[1]] [[1]]$result [1] 3.162278 [[1]]$error NULL [[2]] [[2]]$result NULL [[2]]$error [[3]] [[3]]$result [1] 4.472136 [[3]]$error NULL ``` ::: ::: The output includes successful results and captured errors. ### Title: Extracting Nested Elements with `pluck()` #### Objective Retrieve nested elements from a list. #### Steps 1. **Define a nested list**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nested_list <- list(a = list(b = list(c = 42))) ``` ::: 2. **Use `pluck()`**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} value <- pluck(nested_list, "a", "b", "c") value ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 42 ``` ::: ::: ## Advanced Features ### Customization Customize outputs with `map_*` variants: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Return a vector instead of a list numbers <- list(1, 2, 3) squared <- map_dbl(numbers, ~ .x^2) squared ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 4 9 ``` ::: ::: ### Integration Combine `purrr` with `dplyr` for tidy workflows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) data <- tibble(x = list(1:5, 6:10, 11:15)) # Apply a function to each list element data |> mutate(mean_x = map_dbl(x, mean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|x | mean_x| |:------------------|------:| |1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | 3| |6, 7, 8, 9, 10 | 8| |11, 12, 13, 14, 15 | 13|
::: ::: ## Troubleshooting and FAQs ### Common Issues 1. **Error: "Object not found"**: Ensure all variables are correctly defined and scoped. 2. **Unexpected list outputs**: Use `map_*` variants (`map_dbl`, `map_chr`) for specific return types. ### FAQs - **Can I use custom functions with `purrr`?** Yes, pass any custom or anonymous function to `map()`. ## Best Practices - Use `map_*` variants for predictable output types. - Combine `purrr` with other tidyverse packages for efficient workflows. - Leverage error-handling tools like `safely()` for robust code. ## Conclusion ### Summary The `purrr` package simplifies iteration, functional programming, and working with nested data. Its consistent syntax and integration with the tidyverse make it an essential tool for R users. ### Next Steps - Explore `purrr`'s advanced tools like `transpose()` and `possibly()`. - Integrate with visualization packages like `ggplot2` for applied analyses. ## References and Resources - [Official Documentation](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/) - [Tidyverse Website](https://www.tidyverse.org/) - [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/) ```{mermaid} %%| label: fig-mermaid %%| fig-cap: "Data Transformation Workflow" %%| echo: false graph TD A["Data Input"] --> B["Apply map()"] B --> C["Iterate over elements"] C --> D["Transform Results"] D --> E["Output List/Vector"] ```
